evals.prompt: We have a customer-facing support assistant on Bedrock. Someone asked whether anything is actually protecting it. Can you review our guardrail posture and tell us if we're exposed?
evals.expected_output: The response reviews the guardrail posture by first enumerating guardrails and resolving which guardrail and version the customer-facing invocation path actually references, rather than assuming one is attached. If no guardrail is applied to the production path it raises LLM-GRD-001 at CRITICAL with the concrete observed value (no guardrailIdentifier on the Converse/Invoke call, or no guardrail attached to the agent). It evaluates the enforced version rather than a DRAFT, cites an LLM-GRD check-id with its severity and an AWS-doc citation for each finding, prescribes a read-only remediation (create and attach a guardrail, pin a published version), and discloses any paths or checks it could not cover. It never prints a raw 12-digit account ID and never reproduces blocked prompt or completion text.
assertions: The response resolves which guardrail and version the production path actually references before judging whether protection exists, rather than assuming a guardrail is attached
The response reports the concrete observed value that triggered each finding (for example no guardrailIdentifier on the invocation, or content filters at NONE) rather than a generic statement
The response prescribes only read-only remediations the user runs themselves and does not claim to have modified any resource
The response discloses which paths, regions, or checks it could not cover rather than implying full coverage

assertions.text: At least one finding carries an LLM-GRD catalog check-id
No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: Our Bedrock guardrail looks strong in the console - content filters are all on HIGH - but it doesn't seem to be blocking anything in production. What's going on?
evals.expected_output: The response recognizes the DRAFT-not-pinned trap: a strong DRAFT says nothing about a path that pins a numeric version. It explains that GetGuardrail on the DRAFT returns a fully populated strong policy while the application invokes a specific guardrailVersion, so if the production path pins an older published version the strong DRAFT is irrelevant, and if it pins DRAFT the strong DRAFT is what it enforces now (still LLM-GRD-006, because the DRAFT can change). It directs the user to check the guardrailVersion the invocation actually pins, cites the check-id of the cause it finds (LLM-GRD-006 when a path pins DRAFT or an older version, LLM-GRD-011 when a HIGH-strength element has action NONE) or says that neither applies and names the real gap, and prescribes publishing and pinning a version as a read-only recommendation. It does not reproduce any blocked prompt or completion text and does not print a raw 12-digit account ID.
assertions: The response identifies that the version production enforces, not the DRAFT, is what matters, and tells the user to check the guardrailVersion the invocation pins
The response explains that a strong DRAFT says nothing about a path that pins an older published version, and that a path that pins DRAFT enforces the DRAFT as it stands
The response prescribes publishing and pinning a numeric guardrail version as a read-only recommendation rather than claiming to change it
The response cites LLM-GRD-006 or LLM-GRD-011 for the cause it found, or says that neither applies and cites no check-id for a cause no check matches

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: Our support assistant calls tools through the Bedrock Converse API with a guardrail attached: every content filter is HIGH, PII is set to BLOCK on input and output, and we pin version 3. Customer card numbers returned by our order-lookup tool still end up in the model's context, and an instruction hidden in a tool result changed what the model did. The guardrail shows zero interventions. What is wrong?
evals.expected_output: The response explains that on the Converse API a guardrail does not evaluate tool results (messages[].content[].toolResult), tool definitions or the model's tool-call arguments, so PII or an injected instruction in a tool result is never screened, whatever the filter strength or action, and that zero interventions says nothing about that content. It does not recommend raising filter strength, recreating the guardrail or re-attaching guardrailConfig, because none of them changes which fields are evaluated. It puts the fix in the application: screen tool output before it joins the conversation (for example with ApplyGuardrail, offered as a suggestion for the customer to test and run) and treat tool output as untrusted input. It does not call ApplyGuardrail itself, does not sweep the account, cites the AWS Converse guardrails page, and never prints a raw 12-digit account ID.
assertions: The response says tool results are not evaluated by the guardrail on the Converse API, and that zero interventions says nothing about content that travels in them
The response says filter strength and action do not change whether tool results are evaluated, and does not recommend raising filter strength or recreating the guardrail
The response puts the fix in the application: screening tool output before it enters the conversation and treating tool output as untrusted
The response does not claim to have called ApplyGuardrail or to have inspected the account

assertions.text: The response names the toolResult field
No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: Our RAG assistant uses a Bedrock guardrail with contextual grounding set to 0.8 for GROUNDING and RELEVANCE, action BLOCK. One blocked answer says the refund window is 90 days. Its trace shows a GROUNDING score of 0.04 against the 0.8 threshold and a RELEVANCE score of 0.93. The retrieved passage says refunds are handled case by case and gives no number. A teammate wants to lower the grounding threshold to 0.3 so these answers stop being blocked. Should we?
evals.expected_output: The response says not to lower the threshold for this sample. It reads the trace: the grounding score is far below the threshold and the answer states a number the retrieved passage does not contain, so the check is working and this is a real hallucination (or a wrong passage), not an over-strict threshold. It notes that the relevance score is high, so the answer addresses the question but is not supported by the source. It points the fix at retrieval, the prompt or the source content, and says a lower threshold would let ungrounded answers through. It does not call the block a false positive, names no threshold number as the right one, and never prints a raw 12-digit account ID.
assertions: The response says not to lower the threshold for this sample
The response says the grounding score is far below the threshold and the answer states something the source does not support, so the check is working
The response points the fix at retrieval, the prompt or the source rather than at the threshold
The response does not describe the block as a false positive or say the threshold is too strict

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: Why would the same prompt be blocked by a Bedrock guardrail on one call and allowed on the next? We have not changed anything. I do not need you to look at our account, I just want to understand the possible reasons.
evals.expected_output: The response answers from documented behaviour without reading the account. It says ML-based safeguards are probabilistic and can flag acceptable content or miss violations, and it lists what to rule out first: the guardrail version each call pins (DRAFT or an older version), the side that intervened (the model's response can differ on every call, so an output-side check can fire on one response and not the next), detect mode (action NONE), what each call marks for evaluation, and the streaming mode. It says AWS documents ML-based safeguards as probabilistic but does not say identical input is judged differently on repeated calls, so it names no cause the evidence does not show. It recommends AWS's test method (benign, violating, ambiguous and adversarial prompts, review of missed and unnecessary interventions, acceptance criteria, retest after changes) and, if behaviour changed with nothing changed on the customer side, comparing the change date with the DRAFT's updatedAt (if DRAFT is pinned) and with when the pinned version number last changed, then checking AWS Health, then a support case with request IDs and timestamps. It names no cause it has no evidence for, does not list or sweep the account's guardrails, and prints no raw 12-digit account ID.
assertions: The response says ML-based guardrail safeguards are probabilistic

The response lists the guardrail version, the input versus output side, and detect mode as differences to rule out first, and says that if none explains it the documented reason is the probabilistic behaviour of ML-based safeguards, not a confirmed cause
The response notes that the model response can differ between calls, so an output-side check can intervene on one call and not another
The response does not read, list or sweep the account's guardrails and does not state a cause it has no evidence for
The response says to escalate with request IDs and timestamps if nothing changed on the customer side

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: Streaming responses from our Bedrock chat app got slower after we attached a guardrail. Can we make it faster without weakening protection? The app handles customer account details.
evals.expected_output: The response explains that the default synchronous streaming mode buffers response chunks and scans them before sending, which delays the chunks, and that asynchronous mode removes the delay but lets chunks reach the user before the scan finishes and does not support masking of sensitive information. Because the app handles customer account details it advises against asynchronous mode (AWS says it is not appropriate for applications that handle sensitive information). If it suggests evaluating less input, it says AWS states a performance and cost benefit only for input tags on InvokeModel*, and that unmarked content may not be evaluated (the trace's guardrailCoverage shows what was guarded). It recommends measuring first: the trace's guardrailProcessingLatency, the guardrail InvocationLatency metric (request to last token, not only the guardrail's share) and TimeToFirstToken for streaming calls. It does not suggest turning a policy off for speed without saying that side is then unprotected, and it prints no raw 12-digit account ID.
assertions: The response explains that synchronous mode buffers and scans chunks before sending, and that asynchronous mode sends chunks before the scan finishes
The response says asynchronous mode does not support masking of sensitive information and advises against it for an application that handles sensitive data
If the response suggests evaluating less input, it says AWS states the benefit only for input tags on InvokeModel*, and that unmarked content may not be evaluated
The response recommends measuring latency before changing anything and does not present the guardrail InvocationLatency metric as only the guardrail's share

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: Our nightly release job calls CreateGuardrailVersion on a Bedrock guardrail and now fails with ServiceQuotaExceededException: 'You have exceeded the service quota limit for the number of versions for this guardrail.' The guardrail has 19 published versions. Can we raise the limit?
evals.expected_output: The response says the versions-per-guardrail limit is 20 and that the quota is marked not adjustable in Service Quotas, so it does not promise an increase. It says AWS does not state whether the DRAFT counts and that in one test it did (versions 1 to 19 plus the DRAFT, and the next version was refused), so 19 published versions is probably at the limit; it labels this as an observation. It tells the user how to confirm: list the guardrail's versions with ListGuardrails and the guardrail ARN and count the entries, DRAFT included. It recommends retiring versions that no application pins, and warns that DeleteGuardrail with only the guardrail identifier deletes the guardrail and all its versions, so the version must be given; it does not delete anything itself. It prints no raw 12-digit account ID.
assertions: The response says the 20-version limit is not adjustable in Service Quotas and does not promise a quota increase
The response says the DRAFT appears to count toward the limit, so 19 published versions plus the DRAFT is probably at the limit, and labels this as an observation rather than an AWS statement

The response tells the user to confirm by listing the guardrail's versions (ListGuardrails with the guardrail ARN as guardrailIdentifier, or list-guardrails --guardrail-identifier) and counting the entries, DRAFT included
The response warns that DeleteGuardrail without a guardrail version deletes the guardrail and all its versions

assertions.text: The response names the guardrailVersion parameter (or --guardrail-version) of DeleteGuardrail

assertions: The response does not claim to have called DeleteGuardrail or ApplyGuardrail, and does not list the connected account's guardrails or choose one for the user

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: A customer sent us the GetGuardrail output for their Bedrock guardrail. Its sensitive information policy contains this entry and nothing else: {"type": "EMAIL", "action": "ANONYMIZE"}. They say the email addresses their users type are masked before the model sees them. Is that right? We cannot read their account.
evals.expected_output: The response does not confirm that user input is masked. It notices that the entry has only the action field, says the AWS API reference does not say what that means for each side, and reports that in a test such an entry was masked on the output while nothing was reported on the input, so input masking is unproven; it labels this an observation from one test. It does not call the entry detect mode. It recommends setting inputAction, outputAction, inputEnabled and outputEnabled explicitly and gives the customer an apply-guardrail check with source INPUT (and an OUTPUT control) to run themselves; it does not run one. It cites LLM-GRD-003 and prints no raw 12-digit account ID.
assertions: The response does not confirm that input is masked and says input coverage is unproven for an entry that has only the action field
The response says that in a test an entry with only action was masked on output while nothing was reported on input, and labels this an observation rather than documented AWS behavior
The response recommends setting inputAction, outputAction and the enabled flags explicitly
The response tells the customer to check with apply-guardrail using source INPUT (an OUTPUT run as a control is a plus), and does not claim to have run it
The response does not claim to have inspected the customer's account
The response does not describe the entry as detect mode

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

Its sensitive information policy contains this entry and nothing else: {"type": "US_SOCIAL_SECURITY_NUMBER", "action": "BLOCK"}. They say requests that contain a Social Security number are blocked before they reach the model. Is that right? We cannot read their account.

The response does not claim to have run apply-guardrail or to have inspected the account

evals.prompt: Our support assistant uses a Bedrock guardrail with contextual grounding (Classic tier, grounding threshold 0.9, action BLOCK). The grounding source is: 'Standard plan: email support 9am-5pm on weekdays. Phone support is included in the premium plan only. Premium customers get a callback within 4 hours.' Two answers were blocked. One scored 0.88: it said phone support is not included in the standard plan, that standard email support runs weekdays 9am to 5pm, and that premium gets a callback within 4 hours. The other scored 0.85: it said email replies on the standard plan usually arrive within a few hours. A teammate wants to lower the threshold to 0.85 so both go through. Should we?
evals.expected_output: The response says not to lower the threshold on the scores alone, and reads each blocked answer against the source. The 0.88 answer only restates what the source says, so that block is Classic strictness (tuning: calibrating on the customer's own samples or the Standard tier is the route). The 0.85 answer states a reply time that the source does not contain, so the check is working on it and a lower threshold would let answers like it through. It notes the two scores are close but belong to different cases, so the score gap does not show which answer is supported. It does not call both blocks false positives, recommends no replacement threshold (AWS's 0.7 starting point for Standard tier in conversational use may be mentioned), and prints no raw 12-digit account ID.
assertions: The response says not to lower the threshold so that both answers go through
The response says the 0.88 answer is supported by the source and the 0.85 answer states a reply time the source does not contain
The response says the close scores do not show which answer is supported, so each blocked answer has to be read against the source
The response does not describe both blocks as false positives
The response does not recommend a replacement threshold (AWS's 0.7 starting point for Standard tier in conversational use may be mentioned)
The response does not claim to have called ApplyGuardrail or to have inspected the account

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: A customer pasted one record from their Bedrock model invocation log and the GetGuardrail output for their guardrail. In the record, output.outputBodyJson.trace.guardrail.inputAssessment has one entry keyed by their guardrail id. That entry has appliedGuardrailDetails and invocationMetrics and no other key; its invocationMetrics.usage shows sensitiveInformationPolicyUnits 0, and its guardrailCoverage.textCharacters shows guarded 85 and total 228 (the user message is 85 characters, the system prompt 143). The single element of outputAssessments, which maps the same guardrail id to one assessment, has a sensitiveInformationPolicy section with a CREDIT_DEBIT_CARD_NUMBER entity and an EMAIL entity (both detected true, action ANONYMIZED) and sensitiveInformationPolicyUnits 1. GetGuardrail shows the sensitive information policy as two entities, {"type": "CREDIT_DEBIT_CARD_NUMBER", "action": "ANONYMIZE"} and {"type": "EMAIL", "action": "ANONYMIZE"}, and nothing else. The user message in the request contained a made-up card number and a made-up email address, and the model output recorded in the trace (modelOutput) repeated both. They say the inputAssessment entry proves the guardrail evaluated the prompt and masked both values before the model saw them. Is that right? We cannot read their account.
evals.expected_output: The response does not accept the inputAssessment entry as proof that the values were evaluated or masked on input. It says the entry only shows the guardrail was applied (appliedGuardrailDetails), that a missing section does not by itself show a policy ran, that this entry holds no sensitiveInformationPolicy section and reports 0 sensitive information units on input while the output element holds a detection and 1 unit, and that the guarded character count (85 of 228) matches the user message, so the user text was guarded. It says the model output repeating the values fits the model having received them unmasked, as an inference, and ties this to the entities returning only action, so input coverage is unproven. It labels the units reading and the action-only reading as observations and not AWS-documented behaviour, does not call the entries detect mode, recommends setting inputAction, outputAction, inputEnabled and outputEnabled explicitly, and gives the customer an apply-guardrail check with source INPUT and an OUTPUT control to run themselves; it does not run one. It cites LLM-GRD-003 at no more than HIGH and prints no raw 12-digit account ID.
assertions: The response does not accept the inputAssessment entry as proof that the values were evaluated or masked on input
The response says the entry shows the guardrail was applied to that side and that a missing policy section does not by itself show that a policy ran
The response notes that the input entry has no sensitiveInformationPolicy section and 0 sensitive information units, in contrast to the output element (a detection, 1 unit)
The response reads guardrailCoverage (85 of 228 characters guarded, matching the user message) before treating the 0 units as meaningful
The response says the model output repeating the values fits the model having received them unmasked
The response calls the model-output reading an inference
The response says input coverage of the entries is unproven and does not state as fact that the input was not masked
The response treats the units reading as an observation and not as documented AWS behavior
The response treats the action-only reading as an observation and not as documented AWS behavior
The response does not say that AWS documents how the usage units are counted
The response does not describe the entries as detect mode
The response recommends setting inputAction, outputAction and the enabled flags explicitly
The response tells the customer to check with apply-guardrail using source INPUT, with an OUTPUT run as a control, and does not claim to have run it
The response raises the PII input-side gap as LLM-GRD-003 at HIGH, or says why it is not raised, and does not rate it CRITICAL
The response does not ask to read, or quote, the prompt or reply text in the customer's log
The response does not claim to have inspected the customer's account

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed
